title: Room for the River

definition.text: A Dutch government plan, run from 2006 to 2015, that protects against floods by giving the country's rivers more space while improving landscape and environment.

facts.text: It followed the 1993 and 1995 floods, when over 200,000 people near the Rhine delta were evacuated.
Measures included moving dykes back, lowering floodplains, lowering groynes, deepening side channels, removing obstacles and building a flood bypass.
A basic package of forty projects had a budget of €2.2 billion.
Its Nijmegen project marked a policy shift from ever-higher dikes toward working with natural river dynamics.

notes: Single-country programme kept because it is the chapter's seed and the standard international example of making room for rivers; demote if the course limits country cases.

definition.text: Planning by water utilities and governments to protect drinking water sources from overuse and contamination.

facts.text: It involves identifying sources, assessing contamination threats, informing the public and acting to remove contamination.
It applies to lakes, rivers and groundwater.
Canada adopted it as part of a multi-barrier approach after drinking water in Walkerton, Ontario was contaminated with E. coli.
Researchers have begun bringing ecosystem service assessments into source water protection.

definition.text: Water that comes from precipitation, including heavy rain and melted hail and snow.

facts.text: It can soak into soil to become groundwater, pond on the surface, evaporate, or run off over the land.
In forests and other natural landscapes, soil and plants absorb much of it.
In cities, unmanaged stormwater causes two main problems: flooding and water pollution.
Hard surfaces let less rain soak in, and drains rush runoff into waterways, causing erosion and floods and leaving little to recharge groundwater.
Most runoff reaches streams, rivers and other water bodies without treatment.
Phosphorus carried in runoff feeds algae and toxic cyanobacteria blooms in lakes.
Stormwater is a major cause of urban flooding.

definition.text: Managing the quantity and quality of stormwater, using both engineered controls and everyday practices known as best management practices.

facts.text: Best management practices include structures such as retention ponds and procedures such as street sweeping.
Technical measures include source control of hazardous materials, retention basins and filters, protecting natural waterways, and nature-based solutions working alongside pipes.
Institutional measures include stormwater user fees or utilities, asset management, updated regulations and community education.
Conventional facilities let particles larger than 40 micron settle out and hold water back to reduce flooding downstream.
Stormwater infrastructure is a costly long-term investment that performs worse as climate, urbanization and rules change.
In the US, the EPA regulates stormwater under the Clean Water Act, but farm runoff counts as nonpoint source pollution and needs no permit.

definition.text: Flooding of land or property in a built-up area when rain or coastal storm surges overwhelm drainage systems such as storm sewers.

facts.text: It can happen whether or not a community lies on a floodplain or near water.
Anything that enlarges impermeable surfaces, such as soil sealing, raises flood risk.
Climate change is expected to make storm surges, heavy rain and river overflow more frequent and severe.
In 2020, floods caused an estimated 6,000 deaths and US$51.3B in damages worldwide.
Where homes have basements, it is the main cause of basement and sewer backups, and chronically wet houses are linked to respiratory illness.
Responses include grey infrastructure, green infrastructure, better drainage and changing land use toward more vegetated open space.

definition.text: The three kinds of urban flood planners distinguish: pluvial (from heavy rain), fluvial (from a river overflowing) and coastal (often from storm surges).

facts.text: Each type has different impacts and needs different mitigation.
Erratic rainfall is expected to make both pluvial and fluvial flooding more frequent and severe.
Coastal cities may be hit hardest by sea level rise and heavier rain.

title: Grey infrastructure

definition.text: Conventional infrastructure such as dams, seawalls, pipes and channels, built of concrete or other impervious materials to control water.

facts.text: It can prevent flood damage and be economically valuable, but models suggest it may grow less effective as climate change intensifies floods.
Grey approaches centralize water in big reservoirs, speed it through pipes and fight it with higher walls, the opposite of sponge city design.
Overuse of grey infrastructure can cause water shortages, pollution and loss of water ecosystem services.

related: Economics of green versus grey infrastructure

definition.text: The financial costs urban floods impose on property owners, businesses and cities.

facts.text: US experts estimate wet basements can lower property values by 10%-25%.
FEMA says almost 40% of small businesses never reopen after a flooding disaster.
Urban flooding is estimated to cost £270 million a year in England and Wales.
In the UK, expected annual surface water damages may rise by £60–200 million under 2–4°C warming.

definition.text: Managing a city's freshwater, wastewater and stormwater together as parts of one river-basin plan.

facts.text: It is seen as a way to achieve the goals of water-sensitive urban design.
Managing the urban water cycle as a whole aims to use resources more efficiently, with economic, social and environmental gains.
Integrated stormwater management can improve runoff quality, cut flood risk and add to drinking water supply.
